newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Dull consumer spend to dent Absa 2H margins.
newsitem.headline: Dull consumer spend to dent Absa 2H margins.

text.p: Amalgamated Banks of South Africa Ltd (Absa) said on Monday its margins would come under pressure in the second half of the financial year as the latest central Bank rate hike forced consumers to cut down on spending.

Chief Executive Danie Cronje said at a presentation of the group's first half results that credit demand had shown signs of slowing even before last week's rate increase, as already high interest rates took their toll.
"Margins are definitely under pressure, we can see that in the first two months (of the new financial year). October was not a good month," Cronje said.
"There is no question, especially with the latest increase in Bank rate, that a decline in the demand for credit is going to be experienced... There is pressure on the individual," Cronje said.

South Africa's Reserve Bank pushed up its key lending rate by one percentage point to 17 percent last Wednesday. Most of the country's commercial banks followed suit on Thursday raising their prime rate by the same margin to 20.25 percent.
Although a hike in rates usually brings relief to margins as banks' interest income rises, Cronje said this would be offset by the cost to banks of a persistently high money market shortage.
"Although the one percent hike may help to alleviate some of the pressure, I believe margins are going to be substantially down in the second six months relative to the first half."
In the six months to September 30, Absa posted a net interest margin of 4.63 percent compared with 4.36 percent in year to March 31, 1996.
Cronje said a high interest rate environment was not in the interests of the banking industry as it resulted in a growing bad debt problem.
"The bad debts experienced at these levels of interest rates is not a good one...Individual customers are trapped."
In the six months to end-September Absa's bad debt charge rose 59 percent to 414 million, boosting it to 0.84 percent of advances up from 0.60 for the whole of the last financial year.
Cronje said bad debt provisions were expected to ease slightly in the second half of the year, although for the full year they would be higher than last year settling between 0.84 percent and 0.60.
Absa on Monday reported headline earnings per share of 101.0 cents in the six month period from 73.1 a year ago, beating analysts' consensus forecast of 94.6.
Shares added 45 cents to their market value from an opening price of 23.30 shortly after interim results were announced at 0730 GMT. They had since eased to 23.30 rand -- a 20 cent rise.
